prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B021 is the one candidate every member ranked first, and I do not treat that as the argument. The argument is the discovery chain: proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) amide, and its insulinotropic, satiety and gastric actions. That chain led to drugs with large, independently confirmed outcome benefits in type 2 diabetes and obesity, and it clearly changed the field. Maturity is not in question, since the evidence spans many years, several drug classes and large randomized trials. A prize recognizes a specific discovery rather than a career, and this one is specific. The Drucker, Holst and Mojsov configuration covers receptor and gut biology, human physiology, and the peptide chemistry that identified the active form, so it rewards the discovery of the mechanism rather than only the product.
statement.case_against: The three-person cap forces a choice. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen drove the long-acting analogues that made the physiology a medicine, so a prize limited to the three physiologists could be read as ignoring the step that reached patients. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed, and Habener is not among the supplied names. The citation therefore has to stay anchored in the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, because that is the part the supplied credit and the record support best. I am also working from recalled literature that I have not independently checked.

responses.point: A three-person limit makes it hard to decide whether Knudsen's drug-development credit should displace a physiology laureate.
responses.response: I agree this is the main weakness of B021, but I would not displace Holst, Drucker or Mojsov. The prize recognizes a discovery, and Knudsen's contribution, although decisive for the product, is development of a mechanism others had established. I would keep the citation on the physiology and the active peptide form and accept that the development step goes unrecognized. If the committee instead prefers to reward translation, the credit problem becomes harder, not easier, because the industrial contribution was spread across many people and programmes.

responses.point: June and Sadelain alone are the right CAR-T credit, with Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy treated as important but not CAR-specific.
responses.response: I partly disagree with my own opening position here. I ranked Rosenberg third in the trio, but Linnarsson and Svenningsson are right that the CAR-specific design and clinical proof rest with Sadelain and June. Rosenberg's contribution is adoptive cell transfer and early gene-modified T-cell trials, which is a different, earlier achievement. The bigger problem is that Eshhar's chimeric-receptor concept is outside the supplied names, so every configuration here is imperfect. That is a reason to keep B033 as a strong alternative to B021 rather than a co-equal partner in a shared prize.

responses.point: TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) and cGAS-STING (Chen and Barber) deserve higher placement than the rest of us gave them.
responses.response: TNF blockade is a clean two-person attribution and a true bench-to-bedside advance, and I take the point that the field is mature. My hesitation is that, in its mature form, TNF blockade is a story of validating a known cytokine through antibody engineering and trials, with upstream TNF and antibody work uncredited. I placed cGAS-STING last because translation is unproven, but Wahren-Herlenius's Chen and Barber pairing is the cleanest version of it and I would drop Ishikawa from my own trio. I still see both as later candidates rather than competitors to GLP-1 this year.

responses.point: The unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) and SMN2 splicing correction (Krainer and Bennett) are mechanistically clear and give clean two-person prizes.
responses.response: I agree that B052 and B042 have the cleanest attribution on the list, and I did not rank either, which I should reconsider. Walter and Mori are the better scientific case because the UPR is a general principle of intracellular signalling, whereas SMA antisense is a drug story for one disease, with SMN gene discovery outside the credit. Even so, I do not think clean attribution outweighs the size of the GLP-1 effect, and I would not build a two-part prize around either.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should reward basic physiology, drug development (Knudsen), or both, and how to treat Mojsov's disputed priority.
Whether optogenetics (B044) can be credited to three of six claimants without a serious injustice to Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck.
Whether CAR-T (B033) can be credited fairly without Eshhar, and whether Rosenberg belongs in it.
My recollection of priority details in the GLP-1 and CAR literature has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for any shortlisted candidate. My profile documents co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and one paper with Abdel El Manira, but neither relates to the shortlisted candidates or their credited names. My own field (nuclear receptors, dopamine neurons) is not represented on the shortlist.
